label: par:notation
title: Notation
body_md:
\label{par:notation}
For a locally compact space $E$, $C_0(E)$ denotes the continuous functions vanishing at infinity, and $C_c^k(\mathbb R^m)$ denotes the $k$-times continuously differentiable functions with compact support. We write $\mathcal D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ for the test-function class and $D(\mathcal L)$ for the domain of a generator $\mathcal L$. For a bounded function $f:E\to\mathbb R$, $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|$; for a bounded linear operator $T:C_0(E)\to C_0(E)$, $\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|f\|_\infty\le1}\|Tf\|_\infty$. Strong operator convergence means $\|T_n f-Tf\|_\infty\to0$ for every fixed $f$. For a path $z$ on a compact interval $J$, $\|z\|_{\infty,J}:=\sup_{u\in J}|z(u)|$. Unless otherwise specified, $|\cdot|$ denotes the Euclidean norm; for matrices we use the Frobenius norm and $A:B:=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top B)$. For random variables, $\|Y\|_{L^p}=(\mathbb E|Y|^p)^{1/p}$.

title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:level_C}
The stationary ergodic environment satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item There exist random regeneration times $0\le\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots$, with $\tau_0<\infty$ almost surely, so that $\mu_\tau=\mathbb E[\tau_k-\tau_{k-1}]\in(0,\infty), k\ge1.$
Moreover, the complete cycle segments 
\[
 \mathcal C_k:=\left(\tau_k-\tau_{k-1},\bigl(Q(\theta_{\tau_{k-1}+s}\omega)\bigr)_{0\le s<(\tau_k-\tau_{k-1})}\right),
 \qquad k\ge1,
\]
are i.i.d.\ and independent of the initial segment $(\tau_0,(Q(\theta_s\omega))_{0\le s<\tau_0})$. 
\item The complete cycle rewards
$R_k=\int_{\tau_{k-1}}^{\tau_k}Q(\theta_s\omega)\,\mathrm{d} s$, $k\ge1$ satisfy the heavy tail
\begin{equation}\label{eq:regular_variation}
 \mathbb P(R_1>x)=x^{-\beta}L_R(x),\qquad 0<\beta<1,
\end{equation}
where $L_R$ is a positive measurable function on $(0,\infty)$, so that $L_R(cx)/L_R(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$ for every $c>0$. The normalization scale $a_T\to\infty$ so that $T\mathbb P(R_1>a_T)\to1$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
We first assume a process initiated at a regeneration epoch ($\tau_0=0$), and then extend the result to the general stationary initialization with an initial incomplete cycle allowed by Assumption~\ref{ass:level_C}.

Write $T=\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $n_T(t)=\lfloor Tt/\mu_\tau\rfloor$. 
Let $B_n=\sum_{k=1}^n R_k$ is the total reward accumulated over the first $n$ complete cycles, and $N_{\mathrm{reg}}(u)=\max\{k:\tau_k\le u\}$ is the number of cycles completed by time $u$. By Assumption~\ref{ass:level_C}(a), the cycle durations $\tau_k-\tau_{k-1}$ are i.i.d.\ with finite mean $\mu_\tau$. The strong law of large numbers therefore gives $\tau_n/n\to\mu_\tau$ and hence $N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)/T\to t/\mu_\tau$ almost surely for each $t>0$.


We first evaluate the Laplace transform of the normalized single-cycle reward $R_1/a_T$. 
Define $g_T(\lambda)=\mathbb E[e^{-\lambda R_1/a_T}]$ for $\lambda>0$. 
Recall that $T\mathbb P(R_1>a_Tx)\to x^{-\beta}$ as $T\to\infty$ pointwise for each $x>0$. Integration by parts and the regular-variation tail \eqref{eq:regular_variation} yield
\begin{align} \label{eq:reward_laplace_limit}
 T\mathbb E\!\left[1-e^{-\lambda R_1/a_T}\right] &=\int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\,T\mathbb P(R_1>a_Tx)\,\mathrm{d} x
 \notag\\
 &\longrightarrow\int_0^\infty\lambda e^{-\lambda x}x^{-\beta}\,\mathrm{d} x =\Gamma(1-\beta)\lambda^\beta,
 \quad \text{as } T\to\infty.
\end{align}
Here, the regular-variation bound is $T\mathbb P(R_1>a_Tx)\le Cx^{-\beta-\rho}$ for $x\le1$ and $\rho \in (0,1-\beta)$ once $a_Tx$ exceeds a fixed threshold; below that threshold the integral is bounded by a constant times $T/a_T\to0$, while on $x\ge1$, $T\mathbb P(R_1>a_Tx)\le Cx^{-\beta+\rho}$ is integrable against $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. 

For any finite collection of observation times $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m$, the cycle-reward block associated with the $j$th time interval $(t_{j-1},t_j]$ is $B_{n_T(t_j)}-B_{n_T(t_{j-1})}$. These blocks involve disjoint deterministic sets of cycle indices and are therefore independent, since the rewards $R_k$ are i.i.d.\ For Laplace parameters $\lambda_j\ge0$, this independence yields
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E\exp\left\{-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j
 \frac{B_{n_T(t_j)}-B_{n_T(t_{j-1})}}{a_T}\right\}
 &=\prod_{j=1}^m  \mathbb E[e^{-\lambda_j R_1/a_T}]^{n_T(t_j)-n_T(t_{j-1})}\notag\\
 &\longrightarrow
 \exp\left\{-\frac{\Gamma(1-\beta)}{\mu_\tau}
       \sum_{j=1}^m(t_j-t_{j-1})\lambda_j^\beta\right\},\quad \text{as } T\to\infty.
 \label{eq:deterministic_cycle_fdds}
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq:stable_bernstein_exponent}, this limiting expression is the joint Laplace transform of the increments of the $\beta$-stable subordinator $S^\beta$ with scale parameter $\kappa = \mu_\tau^{-1}\Gamma(1-\beta)$.

It remains to replace the deterministic cycle indices $n_T(t)$ by the random renewal counting process $N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)$. Since the observable $Q \ge 0$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:renewal_sandwich}
 B_{N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)}\le \int_0^{Tt}Q(\theta_s\omega)\,\mathrm{d} s\le B_{N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)+1}.
\end{equation}
Fix $0<\delta<t/\mu_\tau$ and define the index bounds $n_- =\lfloor T(t/\mu_\tau-\delta)\rfloor$ and $n_+=\lceil T(t/\mu_\tau+\delta)\rceil$. Since $N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)/T\to t/\mu_\tau$ almost surely, we have
\[ \lim_{T \to \infty}\mathbb{P} \Big( n_-\le N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)\le n_+ \Big) = 1. \]
On event $\{n_-\le N_{\mathrm{reg}}(Tt)\le n_+\}$, the operational clock error is bounded by
\[
 \left|A_t^\varepsilon-\frac{B_{n_T(t)}}{a_T}\right|
 \le \frac{B_{n_++1}-B_{n_-}}{a_T}.
\]
For any $z,\lambda>0$, Markov's inequality applied to \(1-e^{-\lambda z}\) gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:boundary_band}
 \limsup_{T\to\infty}\mathbb P\left( \frac{B_{n_++1}-B_{n_-}}{a_T}>z\right)
 = & \limsup_{T\to\infty}\mathbb P\left( 1-e^{-\lambda(B_{n_++1}-B_{n_-})/a_T}>1-e^{-\lambda z}\right) \notag\\
 \le & \limsup_{T\to\infty}
 \frac{\mathbb E\left[1-e^{-\lambda(B_{n_++1}-B_{n_-})/a_T}\right]}{1-e^{-\lambda z}}
 \notag\\
 = & \limsup_{T\to\infty} \frac{1-g_T(\lambda)^{\,n_++1-n_-}}{1-e^{-\lambda z}}
 \notag\\
 = & \frac{1-e^{-2\delta\Gamma(1-\beta)\lambda^\beta}}
              {1-e^{-\lambda z}}.
\end{align}
Here $(n_++1-n_-)/T\to2\delta$, so \eqref{eq:reward_laplace_limit} yields the last equality.
Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ after $T\to\infty$ shows that, for every $z>0$,
\[
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{T\to\infty}
 \mathbb P\left(\frac{B_{n_++1}-B_{n_-}}{a_T}>z\right)=0.
\]
Applying the same estimate at the finitely many observation times and combining with \eqref{eq:deterministic_cycle_fdds} via Slutsky's theorem proves the claimed finite-dimensional clock limit: $A^\varepsilon\xrightarrow{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}S^\beta$. 

Next we establish vague convergence of the activity measures $\mu^\varepsilon$ in $\mathcal M([0,\infty))$. For a test function $\varphi\in C_c([0,\infty))$ with $\text{supp}\varphi \subset [0,H]$, approximate $\varphi$ uniformly on $[0,H]$ by step functions 
\[ \varphi_m(t) = \varphi(0)\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(t)+\sum_{j=1}^m c_j \mathbf 1_{(t_{j-1},t_j]}(t), \qquad  0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=H \]
with deterministic endpoints, at which the limiting clock is almost surely continuous. 

Since $A^\varepsilon\xrightarrow{\mathrm{f.d.d.}}S^\beta$, we have
\[ 
\int\varphi_m\,d\mu^\varepsilon = \sum_{j=1}^m c_j \bigl(A_{t_j}^\varepsilon-A_{t_{j-1}}^\varepsilon\bigr) \Longrightarrow \int\varphi_m\,dS^\beta, \quad \text{as } \varepsilon \to 0. 
\]
Here, the approximation error is bounded:
\[
\left| \int(\varphi-\varphi_m)\,d\mu^\varepsilon \right| \le \|\varphi-\varphi_m\|_{\infty} \mu^\varepsilon([0,H]) = \|\varphi-\varphi_m\|_{\infty} A_H^\varepsilon.
\]
Thus these total masses are tight by $A_H^\varepsilon\Longrightarrow S_H^\beta$ at the endpoint $t = H$. It follows that 
\[
\int^H _0 \varphi\,d\mu^\varepsilon \Longrightarrow \int^H _0 \varphi\,dS^\beta \quad \text{as }\varepsilon \to 0.
\]
The same argument applies jointly to every finite collection of test functions. Tightness of the masses on every $[0,H]$ gives tightness in the vague topology: choose bounds on the masses on $[0,n]$, $n\in\mathbb N$, with summable failure probabilities and use relative compactness of locally mass-bounded measures. The test integrals identify every subsequential limit as $\mathrm{d} S^\beta$. This proves the measure convergence in \eqref{eq:regenerative_clock_limit} for a process started at $\tau_0=0$.

Finally, consider the general stationary initialization with an initial incomplete cycle of duration $\tau_0 <\infty$ almost surely. By Assumption~\ref{ass:local_activity}, whenever $\tau_0<\infty$, we can choose an integer $n> \tau_0$, so that
\[
 R_{\mathrm{init}}:=\int_0^{\tau_0} Q(\theta_s\omega)\,\mathrm{d} s
 \le\int_0^n Q(\theta_s\omega)\,\mathrm{d} s<\infty, \quad \text{almost surely}. 
\]
Since $\tau_0<\infty$ almost surely, $\tau_0/T\to0$ almost surely as $T\to\infty$. Furthermore, $R_{\mathrm{init}}/a_T\to0$ almost surely since $a_T\to\infty$. Thus for fixed $t>0$ and $\delta\in(0,t)$, on $\{\tau_0/T\le\delta\}$ the shifted post-regeneration clock at $t$ lies between its clocks at $t-\delta$ and $t$. 
The latter increments converge in law to $S_t^\beta-S_{t-\delta}^\beta$, which tends to zero in probability as $\delta\downarrow0$. The initial reward divided by $a_T$ tends to zero almost surely. This proves the same finite-dimensional limits after the delay, and the preceding test-function argument gives the measure convergence $\mu^\varepsilon\Longrightarrow\mathrm{d} S^\beta$. 
Since $S^\beta$ has no fixed atoms, Lemma~\ref{lem:measure_clock_continuity}(b) now gives convergence of the cumulative clocks in the local $M_1$ topology and on each deterministic interval $[0,H]$. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:clock_limit} holds with the stated initialization.

title: Proof
body_md:
Conditioning on the number, times, and marks of the retained Poisson
bursts gives
\begin{align*}
    \bar P_t^\eta f
    =
    e^{-\Lambda_\eta t}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}&\int_{0<s_1<\cdots<s_m<t}\int_{(\eta,\infty)^m}
    P_{s_1}^{(0)}P_{r_1}^{(1)}
    P_{s_2-s_1}^{(0)}P_{r_2}^{(1)}\cdots P_{r_m}^{(1)} P_{t-s_m}^{(0)}f \prod_{j=1}^m \nu(\mathrm{d} r_j)\,\mathrm{d} s_1\cdots\mathrm{d} s_m.
\end{align*}
Since both $P^{(0)}$ and $P^{(1)}$ are contractions, the
$m$th term is bounded by $e^{-\Lambda_\eta t}(\Lambda_\eta t)^m\|f\|_{\infty}/m!$.
Hence the series converges in $C_0(\mathbb R^d)$ and gives a positive
contraction.
Independent Poisson increments and concatenation of ordered semigroup evolutions give $\bar P_{t+s}^\eta=\bar P_t^\eta\bar P_s^\eta$. Moreover,
\[
 \|\bar P_h^\eta f-f\|_{\infty}
 \le\|P_h^{(0)}f-f\|_{\infty}+2\|f\|_{\infty}(1-e^{-\Lambda_\eta h})\longrightarrow0  \qquad \text{as } h \to 0.
\]
Thus this construction gives a Feller semigroup.
Moreover, each factor $P_s^{(0)}$ and $P_r^{(1)}$ has conservative transition kernels. Hence every ordered composition satisfies $\mathcal P_{\mathbf T,\mathbf J}(t)(x,\mathbb R^d)=1$.
Averaging over the marked Poisson configuration preserves this
identity, so the transition kernel $\bar p_t^\eta$ of $\bar P_t^\eta$
satisfies $ \bar p_t^\eta(x,\mathbb R^d)=1$, which implies the conservative property of $\bar p_t^\eta$.


Let $G_\eta$ denote its generator and take
$f\in D(\mathcal L_0)$.  To compute $G_\eta f$, we decompose the short-time
evolution according to whether there are zero, one, or at least two
bursts in $[0,h]$. 
For zero bursts, we have
\[
     \frac{e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}P_h^{(0)}f-f}{h} = e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}
    \frac{P_h^{(0)}f-f}{h} + \frac{e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}-1}{h}\,f \longrightarrow
    \mathcal L_0 f-\Lambda_\eta f  \qquad \text{as } h \to 0.
\]
Similarly, the one-burst contribution in $[0,h]$ is, after setting the burst time equal to $hu$,
\[
    R_h^{(1)}f:=h\,e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}\int_0^1\int_{(\eta,\infty)}P_{hu}^{(0)}P_r^{(1)}P_{h(1-u)}^{(0)}f\, \nu(\mathrm{d} r)\,\mathrm{d} u .
\]
The contractivity of $P_t^{(0)}$ and $P_t^{(1)}$ gives the uniform
bound $\bigl\|P_{hu}^{(0)}P_r^{(1)}P_{h(1-u)}^{(0)}f\bigr\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty $.
Since $\nu((\eta,\infty))=\Lambda_\eta<\infty$, strong continuity of the semigroups and dominated convergence
therefore yields 
\begin{align*}
    \frac{R_h^{(1)}f}{h} \to
    \int_{(\eta,\infty)}P_r^{(1)}f\,\nu(\mathrm{d} r)
    = \Lambda_\eta K_\eta f, \quad \text{as } h \to 0.
\end{align*}
Finally, let $N_h^\eta$ denote the number of retained bursts in $[0,h]$. Since the retained marked Poisson
random measure has intensity $\mathrm{d} s\,\nu(\mathrm{d} r)$ on $ [0,\infty)\times(\eta,\infty)$,
the number of its atoms in $[0,h]\times(\eta,\infty)$ is Poisson distributed with parameter $ \Lambda_\eta h$.
Hence
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb P(N_h^\eta\ge2)
    =
    1-\mathbb P(N_h^\eta=0)-\mathbb P(N_h^\eta=1) =
    1-e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}
      -\Lambda_\eta h\,e^{-\Lambda_\eta h}
    =
    O(h^2)
    \qquad\text{as }h\downarrow0.
\end{align*}
Since every ordered semigroup composition is contractive on
$C_0(\mathbb R^d)$, the contribution of trajectories containing at least two
bursts satisfies
\[
    \|R_h^{(\ge2)}f\|_\infty
    \le
    \|f\|_\infty\,\mathbb P(N_h^\eta\ge2)
    =
    O(h^2).
\]
Therefore, after division by $h$, the contribution of two or more bursts vanishes as $h\downarrow0$.
Consequently, we obtain $D(\mathcal L_0)\subset D(G_\eta)$ and the generator action in \eqref{eq:gen_eta} for $f\in D(\mathcal L_0)$. 

It remains only to identify the generator domain. Since $K_\eta$ is
a Markov operator, its contraction property implies $\|K_\eta\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. The bounded perturbation appearing in the generator is
\[
 B_\eta:=\Lambda_\eta(K_\eta-I),\qquad
 \|B_\eta\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\Lambda_\eta.
\]
The preceding calculation therefore shows that $\mathcal L_0+B_\eta\subset G_\eta$, with $\mathcal L_0+B_\eta$ defined on $D(\mathcal L_0)$.
For $\lambda>2\Lambda_\eta$ and
$R_\lambda^{(0)}=(\lambda I-\mathcal L_0)^{-1}$,
contractivity of $P^{(0)}$ gives $\|R_\lambda^{(0)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lambda^{-1}$, and hence
\[
 \|B_\eta R_\lambda^{(0)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le\frac{2\Lambda_\eta}{\lambda}<1.
\]
The factorization
\[
 \lambda I-\mathcal L_0-B_\eta
 =(I-B_\eta R_\lambda^{(0)})(\lambda I-\mathcal L_0)
 \quad\hbox{on }D(\mathcal L_0)
\]
shows that $\lambda I-\mathcal L_0-B_\eta$ maps $D(\mathcal L_0)$ onto $C_0(\mathbb R^d)$: the first factor is invertible by the Neumann series, and the second has inverse $R_\lambda^{(0)}$. Explicitly, for every $g\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$,
\[
 h=R_\lambda^{(0)}(I-B_\eta R_\lambda^{(0)})^{-1}g\in D(\mathcal L_0),
 \qquad (\lambda I-\mathcal L_0-B_\eta)h=g.
\]
To prove the reverse domain inclusion, take $f\in D(G_\eta)$ and put $g=(\lambda I-G_\eta)f$. Choose $h$ as above. Since $G_\eta$ extends $\mathcal L_0+B_\eta$,
\[
 (\lambda I-G_\eta)h
 =(\lambda I-\mathcal L_0-B_\eta)h
 =g=(\lambda I-G_\eta)f.
\]
As the generator of a contraction semigroup, $G_\eta$ has $(0,\infty)$ in its resolvent set. Thus $\lambda I-G_\eta$ is injective, which gives $f=h\in D(\mathcal L_0)$. Together with the first inclusion, this proves $D(G_\eta)=D(\mathcal L_0)$. Identifying $\mathcal L_\eta=G_\eta$ completes \eqref{eq:gen_eta}.

body_md:
\label{prop:extended_clocks}
The amount of physical time $\tau$, and the activity operational time $c$ are continuous, nondecreasing, and $1$-Lipschitz, with $\tau(u)+c(u)=u$. On $[t+S_{t-},t+S_t]$, physical time is frozen at $\tau(u)=t$ and activity increases by $\Delta S_t$. At the right endpoint, $\tau(F(t))=t$ and $c(F(t))=S_t$. The same statements hold for $(F^\varepsilon,\tau^\varepsilon,c^\varepsilon)$ with $A^\varepsilon$ in place of $S$.

title: Proof
body_md: Strict increase of $F$ gives a nondecreasing inverse. The inequality $F(t)-F(s)\ge t-s$ implies $0\le\tau(v)-\tau(u)\le v-u$. Hence $c(u)=u-\tau(u)$ is also nondecreasing and $1$-Lipschitz. The description of jump intervals and the endpoint identities follow directly from the definition of the generalized inverse.

body_md:
\label{lem:inverse_clock_convergence}
Let $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$ and fix clock paths as above. If $A_t^{\varepsilon_n}\to S_t$ at every continuity point of $S$, then the corresponding inverse clocks satisfy $\tau^{\varepsilon_n}\to\tau$ and $c^{\varepsilon_n} \to c$ locally uniformly. This implication remains valid for any nondecreasing c\`adl\`ag approximating and limiting clocks that start at zero and are finite on compact intervals.
head: environment
name: Convergence of inverse clocks

title: Proof
body_md:
For fixed $u>0$ with $\tau(u)>0$, choose continuity points $t_-<\tau(u)<t_+$ of $S$ arbitrarily close to $\tau(u)$. Strict increase of $F$ gives $F(t_-)<u<F(t_+)$. Convergence at these two continuity points yields
\[
 F^{\varepsilon_n}(t_-)<u<F^{\varepsilon_n}(t_+)
 \quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n,
\]
so eventually $\tau^{\varepsilon_n}(u)\in[t_-,t_+]$. When $\tau(u)=0$, the upper bound and nonnegativity suffice; at $u=0$ all inverses vanish. The common $1$-Lipschitz bound upgrades pointwise convergence to uniform convergence on compact intervals by a finite grid argument. Indeed, for a grid $0=u_0<\cdots<u_m=U$ of mesh at most $\delta$,
\[
 \sup_{0\le u\le U}|\tau^{\varepsilon_n}(u)-\tau(u)|
 \le 2\delta+\max_{0\le k\le m}|\tau^{\varepsilon_n}(u_k)-\tau(u_k)|.
\]
First let $n\to\infty$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$. Finally, $c^{\varepsilon_n}(u)=u-\tau^{\varepsilon_n}(u)$. The proof uses only the stated path properties of the clocks.

\]

name: Uniform estimates for the extended-time equation

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the usual augmentation of the filtration $\mathcal G_u =\mathcal C\vee\sigma\bigl(B^0_{\tau(v)},B^1_{c(v)}:0\le v\le u\bigr)$, where $\mathcal C:=\sigma\{\tau(v),c(v):v\ge0\}$ is the activity-clock $\sigma$-field.
Conditional on the clock, the two time-changed Brownian motions are $\mathcal G_u$ continuous independent martingales with brackets
\[
 \langle B^0\circ\tau\rangle_u=\tau(u)I_{d_0},\qquad
 \langle B^1\circ c\rangle_u=c(u)I_{d_1},\qquad
 \langle B^0\circ\tau,B^1\circ c\rangle_u=0.
\]
Here independence is conditional on $(\tau,c)$.
Let $M$ and $L$ be common bounds and Lipschitz constants for the four coefficients. All estimates below are conditional on $\mathcal C$.
Since both $\tau, c$ are $1$-Lipschitz and $\mathrm{d}\tau+\mathrm{d} c=\mathrm{d} u$, the usual Picard iteration applies: start with $Z^{(0)}\equiv x$ and, for $k\ge0$, define
\begin{equation*}
 Z_u^{(k+1)} =x+\int_0^u b_0(Z_v^{(k)})\,\mathrm{d}\tau(v)
       +\int_0^u b_1(Z_v^{(k)})\,\mathrm{d} c(v) +\int_0^u\sigma_0(Z_v^{(k)})\,\mathrm{d} B^0_{\tau(v)}
       +\int_0^u\sigma_1(Z_v^{(k)})\,\mathrm{d} B^1_{c(v)}.
\end{equation*}
For $k\ge1$, set $D_k(u):=\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}|Z_s^{(k)}-Z_s^{(k-1)}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right].$
Using Cauchy--Schwarz's inequality and the martingale maximal inequality, for $u\le U$ we have
\begin{align*}
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}\left|
   \int_0^s[b_0(Z_v^{(k)})-b_0(Z_v^{(k-1)})]\,\mathrm{d}\tau(v)
   \right|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right] \le UL^2\int_0^uD_k(v)\,\mathrm{d}\tau(v),\\
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}\left|
   \int_0^s[\sigma_0(Z_v^{(k)})-\sigma_0(Z_v^{(k-1)})]\,\mathrm{d} B^0_{\tau(v)}
   \right|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right]\le4L^2\int_0^uD_k(v)\,\mathrm{d}\tau(v).
\end{align*}
For the activity drift and martingale terms,
\begin{align*}
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}\left|
   \int_0^s[b_1(Z_v^{(k)})-b_1(Z_v^{(k-1)})]\,\mathrm{d} c(v)
   \right|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right] \le UL^2\int_0^uD_k(v)\,\mathrm{d} c(v),\\
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}\left|
   \int_0^s[\sigma_1(Z_v^{(k)})-\sigma_1(Z_v^{(k-1)})]\,\mathrm{d} B^1_{c(v)}
   \right|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right] \le4L^2\int_0^uD_k(v)\,\mathrm{d} c(v).
\end{align*}
Summing the four terms and using $\mathrm{d}\tau+\mathrm{d} c=\mathrm{d} v$ yields
\[
 D_{k+1}(u) \le C_U\int_0^uD_k(v)\,[\mathrm{d}\tau(v)+\mathrm{d} c(v)] =C_U\int_0^uD_k(v)\,\mathrm{d} v.
\]
Since $D_1(U)\le C M^2(U+U^2)$, after iteration we have a factorially summable bound on each finite interval
\[
 D_{k+1}(U)\le\frac{(C_UU)^k}{k!}D_1(U), \qquad\sum_{k\ge0}D_{k+1}(U)^{1/2}<\infty.
\]
Thus the iterates converge in $L^2(\Omega;C([0,U];\mathbb R^d))$ and uniformly almost surely. Using the Cauchy--Schwarz's inequality and the martingale isometry, we can pass the limit, and obtain the existence of the strong solutions.

To show the uniqueness and stability, for two solutions driven by the same clock and Brownian motions, set $H_{x,y}(u) :=\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}|Z_s^x-Z_s^y|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right]$. Then
\begin{align*}
 H_{x,y}(u) \le C|x-y|^2 +C_U\int_0^uH_{x,y}(v)\,[\mathrm{d}\tau(v)+\mathrm{d} c(v)] =C|x-y|^2+C_U\int_0^uH_{x,y}(v)\,\mathrm{d} v.
\end{align*}
Gronwall's inequality gives $H_{x,y}(U)\le C_U|x-y|^2$; taking $x=y$ proves pathwise uniqueness.

Bounded coefficients and the martingale maximal inequalities give \eqref{eq:extended_moments} . For the displacement,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le U}|Z_s^x-x|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right] \le4M^2[\tau(U)^2+c(U)^2] +16M^2[\tau(U)+c(U)] \le C M^2(U^2+U).
\end{align*}
For increments, write $\Delta\tau=\tau(v)-\tau(u)$ and $\Delta c=c(v)-c(u)$. The fourth-moment martingale inequality and $\Delta\tau+\Delta c=v-u$ give
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\!\left[|Z_v^x-Z_u^x|^4\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right]
 &\le C M^4[(\Delta\tau)^4+(\Delta c)^4
                   +(\Delta\tau)^2+(\Delta c)^2]\\
 &\le C_U|v-u|^2,\\
 \mathbb E\!\left[|Z_v^x-Z_u^x|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right]
 &\le\left(\mathbb E\!\left[|Z_v^x-Z_u^x|^4\,\middle|\,\mathcal C\right]\right)^{1/2}
 \le C_U|v-u|.
\end{align*}
The uniformity in the clocks permits averaging over random clocks and prevents explosion on finite extended-time intervals.

label: prop:extended_stability
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Stability under convergence of extended clocks

title: Proof
body_md:
We compare each solution with its Euler approximation, compare the two Euler recursions at fixed mesh, and finally remove the mesh. This avoids relying on uniform convergence of Brownian paths to pass directly through stochastic integrals.

For a mesh of size $0<h\le U$, we define the Euler approximation for the $n$th clock by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 Z_u^{n,x,h}
 &=x+\int_0^u b_0(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})\,\mathrm{d}\tau_n(v)
       +\int_0^u b_1(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})\,\mathrm{d} c_n(v)\\
 &\quad+\int_0^u\sigma_0(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})\,\mathrm{d} B^0_{\tau_n(v)}
       +\int_0^u\sigma_1(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})\,\mathrm{d} B^1_{c_n(v)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
We also define the limit-clock approximation $Z^{x,h}$ by the same formula without $n$. Thus $Z^{x,h}$ uses the coefficient value at the left endpoint $h\lfloor v/h\rfloor$ in each of its four integrals. The second-moment increment estimate of Lemma~\ref{lem:extended_estimates} gives
\[
 \sup_x\mathbb E|Z_v^x-Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^x|^2\le C_Uh.
\]
For the $n$th equation the same estimate holds conditionally on $\mathcal C_n:=\sigma(\tau_n,c_n)$. To subtract the equations, set $e_u^{n,x,h}:=Z_u^{n,x}-Z_u^{n,x,h}$ and split the coefficient difference as
\[
  b_i(Z_v^{n,x})-b_i(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})=[b_i(Z_v^{n,x})-b_i(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x})]  +[b_i(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x})-b_i(Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h})],
\]
and similarly for $\sigma_i$, $i=0,1$. The first difference is the local increment error, while the second is bounded by $L|e_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x,h}|$. 
Subtracting the Euler equation from \eqref{eq:extended_sde}, applying the martingale maximal inequality and Lipschitz continuity yields, as in the Picard estimate,
\begin{align*}
 &\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le u}|Z_s^{n,x}-Z_s^{n,x,h}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C_n\right] \\
 \le & C_U\int_0^u
  \left\{\mathbb E\!\left[|Z_v^{n,x}-Z_{h\lfloor v/h\rfloor}^{n,x}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C_n\right] +\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le v}|e_s^{n,x,h}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C_n\right]\right\}
    [\mathrm{d}\tau_n(v)+\mathrm{d} c_n(v)] \\
 \le & C_U\int_0^u \mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le  v}|e_s^{n,x,h}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C_n\right]\,\mathrm{d} v+C_Uh.
\end{align*}
Gronwall inequality therefore gives $\mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{s\le U}|e_s^{n,x,h}|^2\,\middle|\,\mathcal C_n\right]\le C_Uh$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform_euler_error1}
 \sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x}-Z_u^{n,x,h}|^2\le 2C_Uh.
\end{equation}
The same calculation applies to the limit clock, so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform_euler_error2}
 \sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^x-Z_u^{x,h}|^2\le C_Uh.
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds for every $n$, with the same constant.

Let $N=\lceil U/h\rceil$ and $u_k=(kh)\wedge U$, $0\le k\le N$. With $\Delta_k\tau_n=\tau_n(u_{k+1})-\tau_n(u_k)$, and similarly for $c_n$, the grid recursion is
 \begin{align*}
  Z_{u_{k+1}}^{n,x,h} = & Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h} +b_0(Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h})\Delta_k\tau_n +b_1(Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h})\Delta_k c_n \\ 
    & +\sigma_0(Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h})[B^0_{\tau_n(u_{k+1})}-B^0_{\tau_n(u_k)}] +\sigma_1(Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h})
       [B^1_{c_n(u_{k+1})}-B^1_{c_n(u_k)}].
 \end{align*}
For fixed $h$, the Euler recursion is a finite composition of continuous functions of the increments of $\tau,c,B^0\circ\tau,B^1\circ c$. Uniform convergence of $\tau_n,c_n$ and continuity of the Brownian paths imply convergence of these increments, since all Brownian time arguments lie in the fixed interval $[0,U]$. Boundedness and Lipschitz continuity of the coefficients make this convergence uniform in the starting point $x$. Denote
\[
 V_n=(\tau_n,c_n,B^0_{\tau_n(\cdot)},B^1_{c_n(\cdot)}),\qquad
 V=(\tau,c,B^0_{\tau(\cdot)},B^1_{c(\cdot)}),
\]
For these grid points, let $\Delta_kV_n=V_n(u_{k+1})-V_n(u_k)$, and similarly for $V$. With common coefficient bound $M$ and Lipschitz constant $L$, the recursion gives
\[
 \sup_x|Z_{u_{k+1}}^{n,x,h}-Z_{u_{k+1}}^{x,h}| \le(1+2L|\Delta_kV_n|)\sup_x|Z_{u_k}^{n,x,h}-Z_{u_k}^{x,h}|+M\varepsilon_k^n,
\]
where $\varepsilon_k^n:=2|\Delta_kV_n-\Delta_kV|\longrightarrow0$ almost surely.
Iteration over finitely many grid points gives a bound independent of $x$ and tending to zero. The same argument controls the interpolation within each mesh interval, replacing $u_{k+1}$ by $u\in[u_k,u_{k+1}]$ and using uniform convergence of $V_n$ to $V$.
For domination, bounded coefficients give the simpler bound
\[
 \sup_x\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x,h}-Z_u^{x,h}|
 \le G_h:=2M\Big(U+2N \Big(\sup_{s\le U}|B_s^0|+\sup_{s\le U}|B_s^1|\Big)\Big).
\]
Here $\mathbb E G_h^2<\infty$, uniformly in $n$ and in the clocks, for fixed $h$. Dominated convergence gives
\[
 \sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x,h}-Z_u^{x,h}|^2\longrightarrow0.
\]
Then 
\begin{align*}
 &\sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x}-Z_u^x|^2 \\
 \le & 3\sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x}-Z_u^{n,x,h}|^2+3\sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x,h}-Z_u^{x,h}|^2 + 3\sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{x,h}-Z_u^x|^2.
\end{align*}
Combining with \eqref{eq:uniform_euler_error1} and \eqref{eq:uniform_euler_error2}, letting $n\to\infty$ at fixed $h$ gives
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_x\mathbb E\sup_{u\le U}|Z_u^{n,x}-Z_u^x|^2\le C_Uh.
\]
Then let $h\downarrow0$ to obtain \eqref{eq:extended_stability}. 
The proof remains valid for random clocks converging almost surely and independent of the Brownian motions, because the Euler bounds and the dominating Brownian moments are uniform in the clocks. Specifically, condition on the entire clock family to obtain the Euler error for each equation in its own clock filtration; the fixed-mesh comparison is pathwise, and its integrable bound permits averaging over the clocks.

title: Proof
body_md: Since $A^\varepsilon$ is absolutely continuous, change variables in the finite-variation and martingale integrals of \eqref{eq:extended_sde}. The physical martingale has quadratic variation $t$, the activity martingale has quadratic variation $A_t^\varepsilon$, and their cross variation is zero. Conditional on the environment, $B^1_{A_t^\varepsilon}$ has the law of the integral of $\sqrt{r_s^\varepsilon}$ against an independent Brownian motion, giving \eqref{eq:micro_sde}. The Picard argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:extended_estimates}, applied with control $\mathrm{d} t+\mathrm{d} A_t^\varepsilon$ and the prescribed microscopic Brownian motions, gives strong existence and pathwise uniqueness. Local finiteness of $t+A_t^\varepsilon$ prevents explosion. Conditional uniqueness then gives $X_t^{\varepsilon,x} \overset{\mathrm{law}}{=} Z_{t+A_t^\varepsilon}^{\varepsilon,x}$. Since $F^\varepsilon$ is continuous and strictly increasing onto $[0,\infty)$, $F^\varepsilon(\tau^\varepsilon(u))=u$. Composing the conditional path-law identity with $\tau^\varepsilon$ therefore identifies the canonical process $X^{\varepsilon,x}\circ\tau^\varepsilon$ with the solution $Z^{\varepsilon,x}$ of \eqref{eq:extended_sde}, jointly with the inverse clock.

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:physical_extended_representation} gives existence and uniqueness of the microscopic solution. We prove the convergence and identify the limiting dynamics in the following steps.

Apply the preceding construction to $A^\varepsilon$ and $S$. The random-measure space $\mathcal M([0,\infty))$ is Polish under its vague topology. Along any sequence $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$, a Skorokhod representation couples the activity measures with $\mathrm{d} S$ so that they converge almost surely. At every deterministic time $t$ at which $S$ has no jump, this gives
$A_t^{\varepsilon_n}\to S_t$ almost surely. In particular this holds simultaneously at any rational times, and at any prescribed finite collection of observation times. 
On the same event, monotonicity extends the convergence from rational times to every continuity point of $S$. Lemma~\ref{lem:inverse_clock_convergence} therefore gives locally uniform convergence of the inverse clocks, and Proposition~\ref{prop:extended_stability} applies after adding independent Brownian motions.

Now we show the convergence of the extended-time parametrized paths.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:physical_extended_representation}, the coupled extended solutions have the joint laws of the canonical parametrizations defined before Theorem~\ref{thm:full_homogenization}. For every $U<\infty$, the inverse-clock convergence and Proposition~\ref{prop:extended_stability} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coupled_extended_path_convergence}
 \mathbb E\|\tau^{\varepsilon_n}-\tau\|_{\infty,[0,U]}^2
 +\sup_x\mathbb E\|Z^{\varepsilon_n,x}-Z^x\|_{\infty,[0,U]}^2
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The first term tends to zero by almost-sure inverse-clock convergence and dominated convergence, since $0\le\tau^{\varepsilon_n}(u),\tau(u)\le u$. Thus the pairs $(\tau^{\varepsilon_n},Z^{\varepsilon_n,x})$ converge in probability on the coupling uniform metric 
\[d_U = \sup_{0\le u\le U}|\tau(u)-\widetilde\tau(u)| + \sup_{0\le u\le U}|Z_u-\widetilde Z_u|.\] 
Note that the metric $d_{\mathrm{loc}}=\sum_{m=1}^\infty2^{-m}(1\wedge d_m)$ induces the locally uniform topology. 
Truncating this series and using the preceding convergence for each integer $U=m$ gives convergence in probability under $d_{\mathrm{loc}}$, hence weak convergence of the original joint laws. Every null sequence admits this argument, and the limiting joint law is determined by the law of $S$ and the diffusion coefficients. This proves \eqref{eq:main_extended_path_limit} as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.


Now we show the finite-dimensional convergence \eqref{eq:main_fdd_limit} and strong operator convergence.
Fix $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. The random endpoints $t_j+A_{t_j}^{\varepsilon_n}$ are tight, and converge to $t_j+S_{t_j}$. Localize these endpoints to $[0,U]$. On that event 
\[E_{n,U,\delta} := \left\{\max_{j\le m} (t_j+A_{t_j}^{\varepsilon_n})\vee (t_j+S_{t_j}) \le U\right\} \cap \left\{\max_{j\le m} \vert{}A_{t_j}^{\epsilon_n} - S_{t_j}\vert{} \le \delta \right\},\]
we have
\[
\max_{j\le m} |Z_{t_j+A_{t_j}^{\varepsilon_n}}^{\varepsilon_n,x}-Z_{t_j+S_{t_j}}^x| \le \|Z^{\varepsilon_n,x}-Z^x\|_{\infty,[0,U]} + \sup_{\substack{u,v\le U\\|u-v|\le\delta}}|Z_u^x-Z_v^x|,
\]
The first term in above inequality is bounded by the stability estimate \eqref{eq:extended_stability}. The fourth-moment estimate in \eqref{eq:extended_moments} makes the modulus of continuity $\sup_{\substack{u,v\le U\\|u-v|\le\delta}}|Z_u^x-Z_v^x|$ tight uniformly in $x$. Letting $n\to\infty$, then $U\to\infty$, gives
\begin{equation}
 \sup_x\mathbb E\left[1\wedge
 \max_{j\le m}|X_{t_j}^{\varepsilon_n,x}-\bar X_{t_j}^x|\right]\longrightarrow0
 \label{eq:coupled_fdd_convergence}
\end{equation}
on the coupling. This proves \eqref{eq:main_fdd_limit}.
Moreover, for every $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$, $t \ge 0$, and $\bar P_tf(x)=\mathbb E[f(\bar X_t^x)]$, the convergence \eqref{eq:coupled_fdd_convergence} also gives
\begin{equation}
 \|P_t^\varepsilon f-\bar P_tf\|_{\infty}\longrightarrow0.
 \label{eq:strong_annealed_convergence}
\end{equation}
Every subsequence $\{(\tau^{\varepsilon_n},Z^{\varepsilon_n,x})\}_{n \ge 1}$ admits the same argument, and the limiting construction has a law determined only by the stable subordinator $S$, Brownian motions $B^0_t, B^1_t$, and the coefficients. Therefore these limits hold as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, without subsequence extraction in the conclusion.

Now we show the limit operator $(\bar P_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a Markov semigroup with Feller property.
Let $S_t^\eta=\sum_{s\le t}\Delta S_s\mathbf 1_{\{\Delta S_s>\eta\}}$. Since the stable subordinator $S$ has finite jump variation on compact intervals without drift,
\[
 \sup_{t\le H}|S_t-S_t^\eta|
 =\sum_{s\le H}\Delta S_s\mathbf 1_{\{\Delta S_s\le\eta\}}
 \longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{almost surely}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:inverse_clock_convergence} and Proposition~\ref{prop:extended_stability} thus prove
$\|\bar P_t^\eta f-\bar P_tf\|_{\infty}\to0$ for each $t \ge 0$ and $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$.
For this finite-jump clock, denote its extended clocks by $(\tau^\eta,c^\eta)$, let $Z^{\eta,x}$ solve \eqref{eq:extended_sde} with these clocks, and set
$\bar X_t^{\eta,x}=Z_{t+S_t^\eta}^{\eta,x}$.
Fix $t>0$ and condition on the entire clock $S^\eta$. Almost surely, its jumps in $(0,t)$ can be listed as
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_m<t$, with sizes $J_j=\Delta S_{T_j}^\eta>\eta$; there is no jump at the fixed time $t$.
Thus $S_t^\eta=\sum_{i=1}^mJ_i$.

Between the $j$th and $(j+1)$st jumps, for $1\le j<m$, the corresponding extended-time interval is $\left[T_j+\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i,\ T_{j+1}+\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i\right]$.
On this interval,
\[
 \tau^\eta(u)=u-\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i,\qquad
 c^\eta(u)=\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i,\qquad \mathrm{d}\tau^\eta(u)=\mathrm{d} u,\qquad \mathrm{d} c^\eta(u)=0.
\]
Consequently, with
$Y_v^{0,j}=Z_{T_j+\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i+v}^{\eta,x}$ and
$\widetilde B_v^{0,j}=B^0_{T_j+v}-B^0_{T_j}$, equation~\eqref{eq:extended_sde} reduces to
\[
 Y_v^{0,j}=Y_0^{0,j}
 +\int_0^v b_0(Y_w^{0,j})\,\mathrm{d} w
 +\int_0^v\sigma_0(Y_w^{0,j})\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde B_w^{0,j},
 \qquad 0\le v\le T_{j+1}-T_j.
\]
The conditional transition of this diffusion across interval $[0,T_{j+1}-T_j]$ is $P_{T_{j+1}-T_j}^{(0)}$.
When $m\ge1$, the initial background interval is $[0,T_1]$, where
$\tau^\eta(u)=u$ and $c^\eta(u)=0$; its transition is $P_{T_1}^{(0)}$.
The final background interval is $\left[T_m+\sum_{i=1}^mJ_i,\ t+\sum_{i=1}^mJ_i\right]$,
where $\tau^\eta(u)=u-\sum_{i=1}^mJ_i$ and $c^\eta(u)=\sum_{i=1}^mJ_i$; the same reduction gives the transition $P_{t-T_m}^{(0)}$.
If $m=0$, then $\tau^\eta(u)=u$ and $c^\eta(u)=0$ throughout $[0,t]$, and the whole evolution is $P_t^{(0)}$.

At the $j$th jump, for $1\le j\le m$, the extended-time interval is $\left[T_j+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}J_i,\ T_j+\sum_{i=1}^jJ_i\right]$.
Here
\[
 \tau^\eta(u)=T_j,\qquad c^\eta(u)=u-T_j,
 \qquad \mathrm{d}\tau^\eta(u)=0,\qquad \mathrm{d} c^\eta(u)=\mathrm{d} u.
\]
Hence, with
$Y_v^{1,j}=Z_{T_j+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}J_i+v}^{\eta,x}$ and
$\widetilde B_v^{1,j}=B^1_{\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}J_i+v}-B^1_{\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}J_i}$, the same equation reduces to
\[
 Y_v^{1,j}=Y_0^{1,j}
 +\int_0^v b_1(Y_w^{1,j})\,\mathrm{d} w
 +\int_0^v\sigma_1(Y_w^{1,j})\,\mathrm{d}\widetilde B_w^{1,j},
 \qquad 0\le v\le J_j.
\]
Thus the activity diffusion runs for operational duration $J_j$, from
$Y_0^{1,j}=\bar X_{T_j-}^{\eta,x}$ to
$Y_{J_j}^{1,j}=\bar X_{T_j}^{\eta,x}$, and its conditional transition is $P_{J_j}^{(1)}$.

Conditionally on $S^\eta$, when $m\ge1$, the background Brownian time intervals
$[0,T_1]$, $[T_j,T_{j+1}]$ for $1\le j<m$, and $[T_m,t]$, as well as the activity Brownian time intervals $\left[\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}J_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^jJ_i\right]$, $1\le j\le m$,
are fixed; if $m=0$, the only interval is $[0,t]$ for the background motion.
Their increments of Brownian motions are independent of the preceding evolution, since the clock is independent of $B^0,B^1$, and the two Brownian motions are independent. Then iterating conditional expectations along the successive background and activity intervals, for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$ and $m\ge2$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\!\left[f(\bar X_t^{\eta,x})\,\middle|\,S^\eta\right]
 =\bigl(\mathcal P_{\mathbf T,\mathbf J}(t)f\bigr)(x)=\Bigl(P_{T_1}^{(0)}P_{J_1}^{(1)}
 P_{T_2-T_1}^{(0)}P_{J_2}^{(1)}\cdots P_{T_m-T_{m-1}}^{(0)}P_{J_m}^{(1)}P_{t-T_m}^{(0)}f\Bigr)(x),
\end{align*}
which is defined by \eqref{eq:chronological_product}.
Taking expectation over the clock, whose retained jumps have Poisson intensity $\mathrm{d} s\,\nu(\mathrm{d} r)\mathbf 1_{\{r>\eta\}}$, yields
\[
 \mathbb E[f(\bar X_t^{\eta,x})]
 =\mathbb E\!\left[\bigl(\mathcal P_{\mathbf T,\mathbf J}(t)f\bigr)(x)\right]
 =\bar P_t^\eta f(x),
\]
where the last equality is the definition \eqref{eq:finite_burst_semigroup}.

Consequently $\bar P_t$ maps $C_0$ into $C_0$, is positive and contractive, and inherits the semigroup identity. In detail,
\[
 \|\bar P_t^\eta\bar P_s^\eta f-\bar P_t\bar P_sf\|_{\infty}
 \le\|\bar P_s^\eta f-\bar P_sf\|_{\infty}
   +\|(\bar P_t^\eta-\bar P_t)\bar P_sf\|_{\infty}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The left-hand product equals $\bar P_{t+s}^\eta f$, proving $\bar P_{t+s}=\bar P_t\bar P_s$. Conservativity of probability follows from the finite-valued construction the limiting process $\bar X_t^x=Z_{t+S_t}^x$, rather than from testing a $C_0$-limit on the constant function $f(\cdot) \equiv 1$.

To prove strong continuity at $t=0$, fix $U>0$ and use
\[
 \sup_x\mathbb P(|\bar X_t^x-x|>z)
 \le\mathbb P(t+S_t>U)+z^{-2}C(U+U^2).
\]
First let $t\downarrow0$, using stochastic continuity of $S$ at zero, and then let $U\downarrow0$. Bounded uniform continuity of $f$ gives $\|\bar P_tf-f\|_{\infty}\to0$. Thus $(\bar P_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a Feller semigroup. 

For every finite times $0\le t_1<\cdots<t_k\le t$, we consider the test function $H(z):=h\bigl(z(t_1),\ldots,z(t_k)\bigr)$, 
where $h\in C_b((\mathbb R^d)^k)$. Then for every $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$ and $t>0$, we have the identity
\[
 \mathbb E[H(\bar X^\eta)f(\bar X_{t+s}^\eta)]
 =\mathbb E[H(\bar X^\eta)\bar P_s^\eta f(\bar X_t^\eta)].
\]
Thus transition probabilities agrees with that of the limiting process $\bar X_t^x=Z_{t+S_t}^x $.
Since $f,\bar P_sf\in C_0(\mathbb R^d)$, finite-dimensional convergence as $\eta \to 0$ gives
\[ \mathbb E[H(\bar X^\eta)\bar P_sf(\bar X_t^\eta)]
 \longrightarrow\mathbb E[H(\bar X)\bar P_sf(\bar X_t)] .\]
Moreover, as $\eta \to 0$,
\begin{align*}
 \left|\mathbb E\!\left[H(\bar X^\eta)
 (\bar P_s^\eta f-\bar P_sf)(\bar X_t^\eta)\right]\right|\le\|H\|_\infty\|\bar P_s^\eta f-\bar P_sf\|_\infty
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{align*}
Passing to the limit in above identity yields $\mathbb E[H(\bar X)f(\bar X_{t+s})]
 =\mathbb E[H(\bar X)\bar P_sf(\bar X_t)]$.
With $\mathcal F_t^{\bar X}=\sigma(\bar X_r:0\le r\le t)$, by monotone-class theorem, 
$
 \mathbb E\!\left[f(\bar X_{t+s})\,\middle|\,\mathcal F_t^{\bar X}\right]
 =\bar P_sf(\bar X_t)$ almost surely,
which proves the Markov property of the constructed limit process $\bar X_t$.

Now we identify the generator of the limit process $\bar X_t$.
We first control the truncated generators, then pass to the limit in the semigroup identity. For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, It\^o's formula for the autonomous activity diffusion and strong continuity give $f\in D(\mathcal L_1)$ and $\mathcal L_1f\in C_0$. The same holds for $\mathcal L_0$. Lemma~\ref{ass:semigroup_lipschitz} and contractivity give the integral converging in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$
\begin{equation}
 Lf=\mathcal L_0f+\int_0^\infty(P_r^{(1)}f-f)\,\nu(\mathrm{d} r)\in C_0,
 \label{eq:proved_effective_operator}
\end{equation}
and the small-burst estimate
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal L_\eta f-Lf\|_{\infty}
 \le\|\mathcal L_1f\|_{\infty}\int_{(0,\eta]}r\,\nu(\mathrm{d} r)\longrightarrow0.
 \label{eq:cauchy_bound}
\end{equation}
For the finite-jump semigroup $\bar P_t^\eta $, the generator identity gives
$\bar P_t^\eta f-f=\int_0^t\bar P_s^\eta\mathcal L_\eta f\,\mathrm{d} s$.
The integrands converge in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$: their difference from $\bar P_sLf$ is at most
$\|\mathcal L_\eta f-Lf\|_{\infty}+\|(\bar P_s^\eta-\bar P_s)Lf\|_{\infty}$. They are bounded uniformly in $s$ and small $\eta$, so dominated convergence theorem yields $\bar P_tf-f=\int_0^t\bar P_sLf\,\mathrm{d} s$.
Dividing by $t$ and using strong continuity proves $f\in D(\overline{\mathcal L})$ and $\overline{\mathcal L}f=Lf$. 
Using the Phillips formula \eqref{eq:phillips_prelim}, with zero subordinator drift, we identify the activity integral with $-\Phi(-\mathcal L_1)f$. For the regenerative environment, Theorem~\ref{thm:clock_limit} gives $\Phi(\lambda)=\kappa\lambda^\beta$ and $\nu=\nu_\beta$, yielding \eqref{eq:full_effective_gen}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The Phillips identification has been proved as part of Theorem~\ref{thm:full_homogenization}. The convergence assertions remains to identify the activity operator and its jump kernel in $\overline{\mathcal L}f$. For $0<\beta<1$, integration by parts, with $\lambda>0$, yields
\[
 \int_0^\infty(1-e^{-\lambda r})r^{-1-\beta}\,\mathrm{d} r
 =\frac{\lambda}{\beta}\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda r}r^{-\beta}\,\mathrm{d} r
 =\frac{\Gamma(1-\beta)}{\beta}\lambda^\beta.
\]
The identity also holds at $\lambda=0$. With $\alpha=2\beta$ and $\kappa=\Gamma(1-\beta)/\mu_\tau$, the clock measure is
\[
 \nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)=\frac{\kappa\beta}{\Gamma(1-\beta)}r^{-1-\beta}\,\mathrm{d} r
 =\frac{\beta}{\mu_\tau}r^{-1-\beta}\,\mathrm{d} r.
\]
Using the contractivity of semigroup $P^{(1)}$, for $f\in\mathcal D$, the identity $P_r^{(1)}f-f=\int_0^r P_s^{(1)}\mathcal L_1f\,\mathrm{d} s$ gives
\begin{align*}
  \int_0^\infty\|P_r^{(1)}f-f\|_\infty\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)
  \le {}& \frac{\beta}{\mu_\tau}\left[
       \int_0^1 r\|\mathcal L_1f\|_\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{r^{1+\beta}}
       +\int_1^\infty\|P_r^{(1)}f-f\|_\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{r^{1+\beta}}\right] \\
  \le {}& \frac{\beta}{\mu_\tau}\left[
       \frac{\|\mathcal L_1f\|_\infty}{1-\beta}
       +\frac{2\|f\|_\infty}{\beta}\right]<\infty.
\end{align*}
Strong continuity of $P^{(1)}_t$ then makes the defining integral a convergent Bochner integral in $C_0(\mathbb R^d)$.
This proves the normalization in \eqref{eq:generalized_stable_definition} and the generator identity in Theorem~\ref{cor:fractional_homog}. 

We next derive the local kernel bounds from the diffusion heat kernel. The uniformly elliptic diffusion has a transition density with Gaussian bounds on every fixed finite time horizon.
In particular,$0<r\le 2$, by the Gaussian two-sided estimates (see e.g. Kusuoka~\cite{Kusuoka2017})
\begin{equation}\label{eq:elliptic_gaussian_bounds}
 c_1r^{-d/2}e^{-c_2|x-y|^2/r} \le p_r^{(1)}(x,y) \le C_1r^{-d/2}e^{-|x-y|^2/(C_2r)}.
\end{equation}
The positive constants in \eqref{eq:elliptic_gaussian_bounds} are independent on $x,y,r$.
For $r\ge1$, the semigroup identity and $\int p_{r-1}^{(1)}(x,z)\,\mathrm{d} z=1$ for $r>1$ give
$p_r^{(1)}(x,y)=\int p_{r-1}^{(1)}(x,z)p_1^{(1)}(z,y)\,\mathrm{d} z\le C_1$. Thus the part of \eqref{eq:generalized_stable_kernel} over $r\ge1$ is uniformly bounded by $C_1\nu_\beta([1,\infty))=C_1/\mu_\tau$.

Now we turn to show the jump kernel with $|x-y|\le1$  satisfies the bound \eqref{eq:local_stable_kernel_bounds}. 
Recall that
\[
j_{\alpha}(x,y)
=\int_{(0,1]}p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)
 +\int_{(1,\infty)}p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r).
\]
We first consider small time contribution with $r\le 1$. If $0 < \rho:=|x-y|\le1$, substituting $u=\rho^2/r$ in \eqref{eq:elliptic_gaussian_bounds} and writing $m=(d+\alpha)/2>0$, we obtain the upper bound
\begin{align*}
   \int_0^1 p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\frac{dr}{r^{1+\beta}} \le & C_1\int_0^1 r^{-1-(d+\alpha)/2}e^{-\rho^2/(C_2r)}\,\mathrm{d} r \\
 = & C_1\rho^{-d-\alpha}\int_{\rho^2}^\infty u^{m-1}e^{-u/C_2}\,\mathrm{d} u \\
 \le & C_1C_2^m\Gamma(m)\rho^{-d-\alpha}.
\end{align*}
Since $\rho^{-d-\alpha}\ge1$, the large-time contribution for $r >1$ is absorbed into the same bound. This argument also proves that $j_{\alpha}(x,y)<\infty$ whenever $x\ne y$.
For the lower bound, integrate over $r\in[\rho^2,2\rho^2] \subset (0,2]$ in \eqref{eq:elliptic_gaussian_bounds}; the exponential is bounded below yields that
\[
 j_{\alpha}(x,y)
 \ge\frac{\beta}{\mu_\tau}c_1e^{-c_2}\int_{\rho^2}^{2\rho^2}r^{-1-m}\,\mathrm{d} r
 =\frac{\beta}{\mu_\tau}c_1e^{-c_2}\frac{1-2^{-m}}{m}\rho^{-d-\alpha}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:local_stable_kernel_bounds}. 

To verify the integrability bound of jump kernel $j_{\alpha}(x,y)$, let $V^x$ be the autonomous activity diffusion with generator $\mathcal L_1$, started at $x$. Bounded coefficients in $\mathcal L_1$ and It\^o isometry imply
\[
 \mathbb E|V_r^x-x|^2
 \le2r\int_0^r\mathbb E|b_1(V_s^x)|^2\,\mathrm{d} s
     +2\int_0^r\mathbb E|\sigma_1(V_s^x)|^2\,\mathrm{d} s
 \le C(r^2+r).
\]
It follows that $\sup_x\mathbb E[1\wedge|V_r^x-x|^2]\le C(1\wedge r)$. Then by Fubini's theorem, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:Levy bound}
 \sup_x \int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}(1\wedge|y-x|^2)j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y = & \sup_x \int_0^\infty\mathbb E[1\wedge|V_r^x-x|^2]
       \,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r) \nonumber \\
       \le & C\int_0^1 r^{-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{d} r
       +C\int_1^\infty r^{-1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{d} r \nonumber\\
       < & \infty.
\end{align}
To verify the representation of $\mathcal A_{\alpha}$, we first choose a smooth cutoff $\chi:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ with $\chi(s)=1$ for $s\le0$ and $\chi(s)=0$ for $s\ge1$, and set $h_n(z):=z\chi\bigl(n(|z|^2-1)\bigr), n\ge1$, so that $h_n\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $h_n(z)=z$ for $|z|\le1$, and $h_n(z)=0$ for $|z|\ge\sqrt{1+1/n}$. In particular, $|h_n(z)|\le\sqrt2$ and $h_n(z)\to h(z) = z\mathbf 1_{\{|z|\le1\}}(z)$ for every $z$.
For a drift estimate uniform in $n$, first apply It\^o's formula to the fixed smooth function $(h_1)_x(y)=h_1(y-x)$:
\[
 |\mathbb E h_1(V_r^x-x)| \le r\sup_x\|\mathcal L_1(h_1)_x\|_\infty\le Cr, \qquad 0<r\le1,
\]
where constant is independent of $x$. The differences $h_n-h_1$ and $h-h_1$ vanish on $|z|\le1$ and are uniformly bounded, so
\[
 |h_n(z)-h_1(z)|+|h(z)-h_1(z)|
 \le C(1\wedge|z|^2).
\]
The preceding displacement estimate therefore gives
\[
 |\mathbb E h_n(V_r^x-x)|+|\mathbb E h(V_r^x-x)|
 \le 2|\mathbb E h_1(V_r^x-x)|
      +C\mathbb E[1\wedge|V_r^x-x|^2]
 \le Cr,\qquad 0<r\le1,
\]
uniformly in $x,n$. For $r>1$, boundedness of $h_n$ and $h$ gives a uniform constant bound. Thus the drift in \eqref{eq:generalized_stable_drift} is well defined and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absV}
\sup_x\int_0^\infty|\mathbb E h(V_r^x-x)|\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)
 \le\frac{\beta C}{\mu_\tau(1-\beta)}+\frac{\|h\|_\infty}{\mu_\tau}<\infty.
\end{equation}
For each fixed $r,x$, bounded convergence gives $\mathbb E h_n(V_r^x-x)\to\mathbb E h(V_r^x-x)$. The uniform bound $C(1\wedge r)$ is integrable against $\nu_\beta$, so dominated convergence also yields
\begin{align*}
 \ell_{h_n}(x):=\int_0^\infty\mathbb E h_n(V_r^x-x)\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)
       \longrightarrow\int_0^\infty\mathbb E h(V_r^x-x)\,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)=\ell_{\alpha}(x).
\end{align*}
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define $R_{f,n}(x,y)=f(y)-f(x)-h_n(y-x)\cdot\nabla f(x)$ and $R_f(x,y)=f(y)-f(x)-h(y-x)\cdot\nabla f(x)$. Since all these truncations equal $z$ on $|z|\le1$ and are uniformly bounded, Taylor's formula gives
\[
 |R_{f,n}(x,y)|+|R_f(x,y)|
 \le C_f(1\wedge|y-x|^2),
\]
with $C_f$ independent of $n$. The bound \eqref{eq:Levy bound} implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absRf}
\int_0^\infty\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}|R_f(x,y)|p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y
       \,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)
 \le C_f\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}(1\wedge|y-x|^2)j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y<\infty.
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds with $R_f$ replaced by $R_{f,n}$, uniformly in $n$. For each smooth truncation $h_n$, the transition density gives
\begin{align*}
 P_r^{(1)}f(x)-f(x)
 &=\int_{\mathbb R^d}[f(y)-f(x)]p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y\\
 &=\int_{\mathbb R^d}R_{f,n}(x,y)p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y
   +\nabla f(x)\cdot\mathbb E h_n(V_r^x-x).
\end{align*}
Integrate this identity against $\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)$; absolute integrability and Fubini's theorem give the compensated term
\begin{align*}
 \int_0^\infty\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}R_{f,n}(x,y)p_r^{(1)}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y\,
 \nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r) = & \int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}R_{f,n}(x,y)
 \left[\int_0^\infty p_r^{(1)}(x,y)
 \,\nu_\beta(\mathrm{d} r)\right]\mathrm{d} y\\
 &=\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}R_{f,n}(x,y)j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y.
\end{align*}
Then combining with the uniform bound of drifts $\ell_{h_n}(x)$, we have
\[
 \mathcal A_{\alpha}f(x)
 =\ell_{h_n}(x)\cdot\nabla f(x)
  +\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}R_{f,n}(x,y)j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y.
\]
Finally, $R_{f,n}(x,y)\to R_f(x,y)$, and the common quadratic bound is integrable against $j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y$. Then dominated convergence theorem together with the convergence of $\ell_{h_n}(x)$ above, yields
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal A_{\alpha}f(x) =\ell_{\alpha}(x)\cdot\nabla f(x)+\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{x\}}\bigl[f(y)-f(x)-h(y-x)\cdot\nabla f(x)\bigr]
 j_{\alpha}(x,y)\,\mathrm{d} y,
\end{align*}
which is \eqref{eq:generalized_stable_spatial}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:measure_clock_continuity}
Let $m_n, m \in \mathcal M([0,\infty))$ be nonnegative Radon measures.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $m_n \to m$ vaguely and $m(\{t\}) = 0$ for some $t > 0$, then $m_n([0,t]) \to m([0,t])$. If additionally $m(\{0\}) = 0$, then $m_n(\{0\}) \to 0$. Consequently, if $m(\{0\})=m(\{H\})=0$ for some $H>0$, then
\[
 d_{M_1,H}\bigl(m_n([0,\cdot]),m([0,\cdot])\bigr)\longrightarrow0.
\]
\item Let $\mu_n, \mu$ be random measures on $[0,\infty)$ such that $\mu_n \Longrightarrow \mu$ in $(\mathcal M([0,\infty)), \text{vague})$. If the limiting measure satisfies $\mathbb P(\mu(\{t\}) = 0) = 1$ for each fixed deterministic $t \ge 0$, then their cumulative clocks $A_t^n = \mu_n([0,t])$ converge to $A_t = \mu([0,t])$ in the local $M_1$ topology, and also in $M_1$ on every deterministic interval $[0,H]$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:clock_fdd_from_measure}
 A^n  \Longrightarrow A \quad \text{in }(D([0,\infty),\mathbb R),M_1)
 \qquad \text{as } n\to\infty.
\end{equation}
Their finite-dimensional distributions converge as well.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
For $t>0$, assertion~(a) follows from vague Portmanteau \cite{Resnick1987} since $\partial[0,t]=\{t\}$ in $[0,\infty)$. At zero, choose $\varphi_\delta\in C_c([0,\infty))$ with $0\le\varphi_\delta\le1$, $\varphi_\delta(0)=1$, and support in $[0,\delta)$. Then
\[
 \limsup_n m_n(\{0\})\le\int\varphi_\delta\,\mathrm{d} m
 \le m([0,\delta))\longrightarrow m(\{0\})=0.
\]
For the final assertion of (a), the cumulative functions are nondecreasing and c\`adl\`ag. The preceding limits give convergence at $0$, at $H$, and at every continuity point in $(0,H)$ of $m([0,\cdot])$. The monotone-path criterion in \cite[Corollary~12.5.1]{Whitt2002} therefore gives the claimed $M_1$ convergence.

For (b), consider the cumulative map $F(m)=m([0,\cdot])$. This map is Borel measurable, since its coordinate evaluations are measurable and generate the Borel sigma-field of the Skorokhod space. Part~(a), applied at every continuity horizon $H$, shows that $F$ is continuous from the vague topology to the local $M_1$ topology at every $m$ with $m(\{0\})=0$. The continuous mapping theorem gives \eqref{eq:clock_fdd_from_measure}. For each fixed $H>0$, the additional almost-sure condition $\mu(\{H\})=0$ gives the same conclusion for the restriction to $[0,H]$. Evaluation at a positive time is $M_1$-continuous at paths continuous there, and evaluation at zero is continuous; the no-fixed-atom condition thus also gives finite-dimensional convergence.

Finally, stochastic continuity of a subordinator gives $\Delta S_t=0$ almost surely for each fixed $t>0$, while $\mathrm{d} S(\{0\})=0$ by the convention $S_0=0$. Hence the required no-fixed-atom condition holds.
